title: Lunge a trained horse for exercise

lessons.title: Preparing a horse for lungeing
lessons.html:
What is lungeing?

Lungeing means exercising a horse on a long rein, called a lunge line, while it moves in a circle around you. It is used to exercise a horse that cannot be ridden that day, to warm a horse up, or to let a fresh horse settle. In this unit you lunge a horse that is already trained.

The place

  • A round lunge ring or a fenced corner of the arena
  • Level ground with good, non-slippery footing; no stones or holes
  • Quiet, away from other horses being ridden

Lungeing equipment

ItemPurpose
Lunge cavesson or bridle (as the yard uses)Attaches the line to the horse's head
Lunge line (about 8 to 10 m)Connects you to the horse
Lunge whipAn aid to send the horse forward
Brushing boots on all four legsProtect the legs from knocks
Roller or saddle with stirrups secured (if instructed)Used for some training

Fitting the equipment

  1. Groom the horse and pick out the feet.
  2. Fit the brushing boots, straps on the outside, done up front to back.
  3. Fit the cavesson. The noseband sits about two fingers below the cheekbone. Make sure it is snug so it does not twist and rub the eye.
  4. If a saddle is used, run the stirrups up and secure them so they cannot swing and bang the horse.
  5. Attach the lunge line to the front ring of the cavesson.

What you wear

Gloves are essential: a lunge line can burn your hands if the horse pulls. Wear boots and a helmet. Do not wear loose clothes or spurs.

Check the horse

Only lunge a horse that is sound and well. If you see lameness, swelling or heat, do not lunge; report it.

lessons.title: Using the lunge rein, whip and voice
lessons.html:
The triangle

When lungeing, you, the line and the whip form a triangle with the horse. The line goes to the horse's head, the whip points towards its hindquarters, and you stand at the point of the triangle in the middle of the circle. Your body should be level with the horse's shoulder or slightly behind it.

Holding the lunge line

  • Hold the line in the hand on the direction you are going: left hand when the horse goes to the left (anti-clockwise).
  • Fold the spare line in loops across your hand, never wrapped around it. If the horse pulls, the loops slide out instead of trapping your hand.
  • Keep a light, even contact. The line should not drag on the ground or be pulled tight.

The lunge whip

Hold the whip in the other hand, pointing towards the horse's hocks, with the lash trailing. The whip is a signal, not a punishment. You use it to:

  • Ask the horse to go forward: raise or move it towards the hindquarters.
  • Keep the horse out on the circle: point it towards the shoulder.
  • Slow down: lower the whip and point it behind you.

Never hit the horse with the whip. When changing direction or going to the horse, turn the whip so it points behind you, under your arm.

Voice commands

CommandHow to say it
"Walk on"Clear and bright
"Trot on" / "Te-rot"Upward, encouraging
"And canter"Sharp, rising
"Whoa" / "Walk"Long, low and calm
"Stand"Low, firm

Upward, sharp tones ask the horse to go faster. Long, low, slow tones ask it to slow down. Use the same words the horse was trained with; ask your supervisor.

Body language

If you step towards the horse's hindquarters, it goes forward. If you step towards its head, it slows or stops. Keep your body calm and still otherwise.

lessons.title: Lungeing for exercise and putting away the tack
lessons.html:
Conducting the session

  1. Lead the horse into the lunge area and close the gate.
  2. Stand the horse on the track. Let out a little line, step back towards the centre and ask "walk on".
  3. Let out more line gradually until the horse walks on a large circle.
  4. Walk a few rounds to warm up.
  5. Ask for trot. Keep it steady and even.
  6. Change direction regularly, about every five minutes, so both sides work equally.
  7. End with walk to cool down.

Your yard will tell you how long to lunge. Lungeing is hard work for the horse's legs because of the circle, so sessions are kept fairly short, usually under half an hour, and the circle must not be too small.

Changing direction

Ask the horse to halt on the circle. Turn the whip behind you. Walk up the line to the horse, folding the line as you go. Change the line to the other side, then send the horse off on the new rein.

Watch the horse

  • Is it moving evenly, or is it lame?
  • Is it calm, or rushing and pulling?
  • Is it breathing too hard or sweating heavily?

If the horse becomes lame, distressed or uncontrollable, ask it to slow down and stop, and report to your supervisor.

If the horse pulls away

Let the line slide through your gloved hand rather than being dragged. Never wrap it around your hand or body. Stay calm, stand still, and the trained horse will usually stop. Catch it quietly.

After lungeing

  1. Bring the horse in, fold the line, and lead the horse out of the area.
  2. Remove the line, cavesson, roller and boots in the stable.
  3. Check legs for heat or knocks. Brush off sweat marks.
  4. Clean the tack: wipe leather with a damp cloth and saddle soap; brush mud off boots.
  5. Coil the lunge line neatly in loops or a figure of eight so it does not tangle.
  6. Hang the whip upright or on its rack so it does not bend.
  7. Store everything in its place in the tack room.

Key points

  • Use a safe lunge area, boots on the horse, and gloves and helmet on you.
  • Line, whip and you form a triangle; stand level with the shoulder.
  • Fold the line in loops; never wrap it around your hand.
  • Sharp, rising voice to go forward; long, low voice to slow down.
  • Change direction regularly, keep sessions short, and clean and store tack after.
